activities.caption: rebuild the engineering pipeline — code first, pipette last
activities.name: bioGMPipelineOrder

config.prompt: A genetic-modification project, read as information engineering — put the stations in order:
items: Find the gene's sequence in the databases (GenBank, Ensembl)
Design the construct: restriction-site planning, codon optimisation in software
Simulate the cloning in silico — the circular construct assembled before any enzyme moves
Verify by sequencing the edited genome and aligning it back to the plan
The wet lab runs — the last mile of a pipeline whose first ninety percent is code
config.why: Every modification is a data operation: find, design, simulate, verify — with guide-RNA design itself a fuzzy string-matching problem scored and ranked by software.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — one genome's weight in text
activities.name: bioGenomeEstimate

config.prompt: A sequencer's output is text: FASTA files of A, C, G, T. Once processed, roughly how large is one human genome?
config.why: ~100 GB of processed text per genome — terabytes arrive daily, which is why biology became a data science by arithmetic.
config.context: Sanger took 13 years and about 3 billion dollars for one draft genome; Illumina reads millions of fragments in parallel for a few hundred to a thousand dollars.

activities.anchor: reading it is a first-day skill
activities.caption: fill the blanks — reading the quality metadata
activities.name: bioPhredCloze

config.text: Each base arrives with a Phred score, Q = −10 log₁₀(p), where p is the probability the base call is %%0%%. Q30 means %%1%%% accuracy, and Q40 means one error in every %%2%% bases. Pipelines filter and trim on these scores before any %%3%% is attempted, because garbage %%4%%: a single bad base can misjoin contigs.
config.hint: The score is ten times the log of the error probability — every ten points is another decimal place of accuracy.

activities.caption: pair each alignment tool with its trade
activities.name: bioAlignMatch

config.prompt: The alignment toolbox — pair each entry with what it does:

pairs.right: local alignment — the best matching stretch only
short exact seeds first, then extend only the promising ones

pairs.left: a region conserved across many species
pairs.right: clue to an essential function — the slower it changes, the more it matters

config.why: The rigorous grid method would take years against a billion-base database; BLAST's engineering trade made search tractable — and became the most-cited paper in biology's literature.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the assembly answer
activities.name: bioAssemblySpot

config.prompt: This genome-assembly answer contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Sequencers output fragments, not genomes — assembly stitches them back together.
Short-read assemblers break reads into k-mers and build a de Bruijn graph of overlaps.
Walking the graph produces contigs; long reads bridge the repeats and close the gaps.
The first human 'complete' genome in 2003 was finished telomere-to-telomere, with no gaps.
Annotation then labels genes, regulatory elements and selfish repeats — about half the human genome.
config.correction: The 2003 genome was a mosaic of hundreds of gaps — the last centromeres and satellite arrays fell only in 2022, to the Telomere-to-Telomere consortium's long reads.
config.why: Repeats where all pieces look identical are what defeat short reads; unreadable for twenty years, the final gaps needed long-molecule sequencing to resolve.

activities.caption: file the results by the tool that produced them
activities.name: bioToolBuckets

config.prompt: Three workhorses, six results — file each by the tool that did the job:

items.label: whales sit inside the even-toed ungulates
HIV jumped from chimpanzees early in the twentieth century
gene-finding was the first large-scale ML problem in biology
annotators predicting gene structure from sequence with neural networks
k-mers walked into contigs through a de Bruijn graph
SARS-CoV-2 samples placed on the evolving tree within days

config.why: Alignment builds the tree; machine learning labels the assembly; graph theory stitches the reads — the pipeline's three engines.

activities.anchor: read directly from fossils and guesses
activities.caption: true or false — what a tree actually is
activities.name: bioTreeJudge

statements.s: Every published tree is a computed estimate from aligned sequence data under a model of molecular evolution.
statements.why: Different models and gene choices give different trees — inference with quantified confidence.

statements.s: Horizontal gene transfer makes bacterial gene trees agree perfectly with species trees.
statements.why: It scrambles the picture — bacteria exchange genes sideways, drawing the deepest ancestor as a web, not a trunk.

statements.s: Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry their own genomes from different ancestors.
statements.why: Genes have histories that can differ from species histories.

statements.s: 'The' tree of life is a consensus of thousands of gene trees, some of which disagree productively.
statements.why: The disagreement is data — productive conflict, not embarrassment.

activities.anchor: resisted everyone for half a century
activities.caption: before and after CASP14 — the 50-year problem
activities.name: bioFoldCompare

config.prompt: Protein structure prediction — drag the divider across 2020:

before.label: before CASP14
before.text: Computing the fold from sequence resisted everyone for half a century — the fold follows from physics (Anfinsen), but the calculation defeated biology's grand challenge.

after.label: after AlphaFold2
after.text: Trained on 170,000 known structures, attention networks reasoning over residue pairs — 200+ million predicted structures, free for all, structure effectively solved for single chains.

config.why: The 2024 chemistry Nobel went to Hassabis and Jumper. The honest boundary survives: interactions, dynamics and disordered regions are harder — a prediction is a hypothesis, not a measurement.
